description: Group of friends with ambition to compete and learn.
summary: We developed Signal or Noise, a web platform that turns students, teachers and curious citizens into Earth system detectives. On a 3D globe, users pick one of 919 places (glaciers, volcanoes, lakes, deserts, cities, oceans and more) and a NASA variable such as temperature, rain or soil moisture. The platform builds a 45-year series from NASA data, measures how fast it changes, and tests whether the change is real or just chance. Most tools stop at a trend line; ours gives an honest verdict (Confirmed, Likely or Not yet known) and, when a trend is not yet clear, estimates how many more years of data would settle it. Users make the calls themselves, open clues like detectives and earn points, alone or in a classroom competition with a QR code and a live leaderboard. A global monitor shows where the planet is changing: NASA data show it warming +0.17 °C per decade since 1981, and the Arctic +0.44 °C. A Moon mode explores how the Moon affects the Earth, from proven tides to open questions such as the 18.6-year lunar cycle and glaciers. Climate news is full of trends; this platform teaches people to ask: is this signal, or noise?
details:
Is the place where you live really changing, or are you looking at noise?

High above Arequipa, Peru, stands Nevado Coropuna, a volcano covered by an ice cap. Every year its air is a little warmer or a little colder than the year before. One year tells you nothing. Forty-five years of NASA data, tested the right way, tell you a lot: the air around Coropuna is warming +0.24 °C per decade, and that trend has been statistically clear since 2006.

Climate data is open to everyone, but a wiggly curve fools the eye: people see trends that are not there and miss the ones that are. Signal or Noise puts a real statistical test in anyone's hands, and it is honest enough to say "we don't know yet".

The home screen: a 3D globe, three paths, and the visitor's own country first.

What exactly does it do?

Three steps, like a detective.

  1. Open a case. Pick one of 919 places (glaciers, volcanoes, lakes, deserts, cities, oceans…) or any point on the globe, and one of 15 NASA variables. First you write down your hunch: will it rise, fall, or stay the same?
  2. Read the evidence. The app draws 1981–2025, one value per year, with its trend line.
  3. Get an honest verdict: Confirmed, Likely or Not yet known. Clues show why: a second statistical test, a prediction test on years the model never saw, an El Niño "alibi" check and, for large regions, a second witness (AIRS satellite vs. MERRA-2 model).

The evidence for Coropuna: +0.24 °C per decade, confirmed.

The verdict and its clues. Each ✓ is a check the trend had to pass.

The clock turns uncertainty into something you can picture: how many more years of data would settle an unclear trend, or since when a clear one has been known.

Beyond one case:

  • Global monitor. 2,592 cells show where the planet is changing. According to NASA data, the whole planet is warming +0.17 °C per decade since 1981, and the Arctic +0.44 °C. Click anywhere to open that spot as a case.
  • Moon mode. A 3D Moon with 1,178 official names and Moon–Earth cases, each opened by an animated Earth–Moon scene. Tides are the proof that the Moon moves the Earth (the 18.6-year lunar cycle appears in all 8 NOAA tide gauges tested); rain and glaciers stay an open question.
  • Classroom mode. A teacher shows a QR code. Students scan it with their own phones, join as anonymous numbered detectives (no name, e-mail or account) and compete on a live leaderboard.
  • For everyone. Six languages (English, Español, Português, Français, Русский, 中文), works on phones, and the globe starts over the visitor's own country.

Global monitor: 67% of the planet shows rising air temperature; faint areas are "not confirmed yet".

A Moon case: why the Moon raises two ocean bulges, tested against 100 years of tide gauges.

Classroom mode: one QR code, a live leaderboard, no accounts.

How does it work? (and how we keep it honest)

  1. Data. NASA POWER (MERRA-2 meteorology, CERES radiation) read live in the browser, with temperature and rain bundled for every place; precomputed MERRA-2, AIRS and GLDAS (Earthdata OPeNDAP), MODIS, Worldview and LRO imagery.
  2. No false trends. Yearly means remove the seasons, and series are cut where instruments changed, so stitching data together never creates a trend.
  3. Statistics. Sen's slope; Mann-Kendall with the Hamed & Rao autocorrelation correction (results match the reference Python library); a t-test as second witness; Benjamini-Hochberg when thousands of map cells are tested at once.
  4. Moon test. A lunar index from astronomy is compared with the data against 999 placebo series (about 5% false alarms). It never says "confirmed", only "Moon-like signal", "a hint" or "none".
  5. Light and verifiable. HTML, CSS and JavaScript with CesiumJS on static hosting; only the classroom uses a free Firebase database, protected by security rules. 23 automated tests check the statistics, and a browser audit clicks through more than 200 interactions at desktop and phone sizes. No AI runs inside the app: every result comes from tested statistics.

What benefits does it have?

  • Students practise the scientific method with real NASA data: hunch, evidence, test, and accepting "we don't know yet".
  • It shows uncertainty instead of hiding it, so trust is earned, not assumed.
  • The game turns statistics into a reasoning challenge: you can be wrong, and you learn why.
  • It starts in Arequipa and scales to the whole planet and the Moon.
  • Free, open source, no login.

What do you hope to achieve?

We want teachers in Arequipa to use it in class, with a live shared leaderboard. The catalogue already covers at least 20% of a cited universe of places for each phenomenon (929 of 4,506 place memberships). Next: full coverage, more NASA instruments, and deeper Moon–Earth research, starting with glaciers, the topic of Alvaro's thesis.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

JavaScript, HTML, CSS and Python (NumPy, Pillow); CesiumJS, qrcode-generator, Firebase (Firestore and anonymous sign-in) and Node.js; Cloudflare Pages and GitHub Pages hosting; NASA POWER, Earthdata, GIBS, Moon Trek, ORNL DAAC, NOAA, Wikidata, Wikimedia Commons, Open-Meteo and USGS services; VS Code, Git/GitHub, Claude Code and Codex (see SI), Orca and Chrome DevTools; one laptop.

Source code (open source): https://github.com/ThatGust/NASA-glaciers-2026-detective Mirror for networks that block Cloudflare: https://thatgust.github.io/NASA-glaciers-2026-detective/
